title: Tracelayer
pitch: Give AI agents useful access, without giving away Human authority.
about_excerpt: Give AI agents useful access, without giving away Human authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration As AI agents become capable of using websites and taking actions on behalf of users, I kept coming back to one question: How do we give an AI agent useful access without also giving it full trust or Human authority? This becomes especially important in high-stakes applications. In cybersecurity, finance, administration, or access management, an Agent may be useful for gathering information and making recommendations, but a wrong action can have real consequences. I did not want to build another cybersecurity copilot that simply reads logs and produces a verdict. Instead, I used a synthetic security incident as a proving ground for a broader idea: a web application should decide what an Agent is allowed to do at every stage, preserve Human context and judgment, and keep consequential authority separate from Agent reasoning. That became TraceLayer . What TraceLayer does TraceLayer is a WebMCP-native reference architecture for Human-Agent collaboration in high-stakes web applications. The demo follows one synthetic cybersecurity case involving suspicious account and connected-application activity. ChatGPT investigates the case using structured tools exposed directly by the TraceLayer webpage through WebMCP. During the investigation, the Agent can read evidence, inspect entities, connect related events, link evidence, and maintain an assessment. But its capabilities are not static. As the case progresses, TraceLayer changes the Agent's WebMCP surface. During investigation, it can gather and record evidence. During response review, investigation writes disappear and the Agent can only read the case and propose a response. Once a consequential proposal is pending approval, the Agent becomes read-only. There is deliberately no WebMCP tool for authorization or execution . The Human also contributes something the Agent cannot determine from the exposed investigation data. In the demo, a login appears to originate from Singapore. The Agent initially treats that location as supporting evidence of compromise. The Human checks an internal company network reference and adds organizational context showing that the address is actually a sanctioned corporate VPN exit. The original event is never rewritten. Instead, the Agent reads the updated shared case and creates a new assessment that supersedes its earlier interpretation. This creates a collaboration loop where: Agent reasoning → Human context → Agent reassessment rather than treating the Agent's first answer as final. Why authentication matters The most important boundary appears when the Agent proposes a consequential action. Simply placing an Approve button on a webpage is not enough. A browser Agent may also be capable of interacting with ordinary webpage controls, so a click by itself is not strong evidence that a Human approved the decision. TraceLayer separates three responsibilities: Agent: investigates and proposes. Human: provides organizational context and authorizes consequential decisions. SYSTEM: performs an approved operation. Signing in with ChatGPT establishes the account identity, but identity alone is still not approval. For consequential actions, TraceLayer uses a fresh WebAuthn user-verification ceremony tied to the exact proposal and current case state. Only after that verification does TraceLayer record the Human authorization. A separate SYSTEM record then performs the simulated security action. In short: The Agent proposes. The Human authorizes. SYSTEM executes. The authorization flow is real. The cybersecurity telemetry and response effects in the demo are synthetic and simulated. How I built it TraceLayer is a browser-first application built around a single shared case state. The Human interface and the WebMCP interface both operate on the same underlying domain functions, so the Agent is not interacting with a separate demo backend or a scripted copy of the case. TraceLayer exposes seven generic WebMCP tools: get_case_state query_events inspect_entity correlate_entities link_evidence record_assessment propose_response_action The page dynamically registers only the tools appropriate for the current stage of the investigation. Application policy remains authoritative even if an Agent has stale knowledge of a previously available capability. The incident contains 40 immutable synthetic events. Some evidence is externally controlled and even contains instruction-like text aimed at automated review. TraceLayer still exposes that content as evidence, but that content does not gain authority over application policy, tool availability, authorization, or execution. The final workflow is: INVESTIGATING → RESPONSE_REVIEW → PENDING_AUTHORIZATION → POST_ACTION_REVIEW → CASE_COMPLETE At completion, TraceLayer produces an inspectable Decision Trail showing what the Agent assessed and proposed, what context and decisions came from the Human, and what actions were performed by SYSTEM. Challenges The hardest part was not getting the Agent to investigate the incident. ChatGPT could solve the synthetic case surprisingly quickly. The harder problem was designing an interaction where the Human genuinely mattered. Early versions risked becoming the familiar pattern of: AI recommends → Human clicks approve That was not enough. The Human needed to contribute knowledge that changed the investigation itself, not just appear at the end as a ceremonial approval button. That led to the organizational-context handoff and assessment-supersession model. Another major challenge was authority. At first, Human and SYSTEM actions were represented only as application-level actor labels. Testing showed that an Agent with normal browser interaction could potentially initiate ordinary UI controls. That forced a much stronger design: authenticated identity, real WebAuthn user verification, exact proposal binding, fresh challenges, replay protection, and separate SYSTEM execution. I also spent significant time trying to break the implementation rather than only proving the happy path. The final project includes tests for stale capabilities, replay attempts, wrong revisions, wrong users, rejected proposals, raw-evidence immutability, deterministic reset, hostile-content behavior, and multi-user authority isolation. The final suite contains 128 automated tests , alongside TypeScript, lint, build, accessibility, responsive, and published-host validation. What I learned The biggest lesson was that Agent capability and Human authority are different things . Giving an Agent access to useful tools does not mean it should inherit the authority of the Human using the application. I also learned that Human-Agent collaboration becomes much more meaningful when both sides contribute something distinct. video_transcript_excerpt: Hello, this is a simulated cybersecurity incident for the demonstration. This is Trace Layer. It explores a simple problem when we let a AI agent use a high-stakes web app. How do we give it useful access without also giving it full trust or human authority? Allow me to demonstrate how it works. Trace Layer uses Web MCP to give ChatGPT a small set of structured tools based on the current case state. When the workflow reaches a consequential action, the agent may propose it, but verified human authorization is required before system execution. Some evidence can even contain instructions like text trying to influence automatic review. Its content alone does not impact the agent's capability or gain authority. The agent reaches an initial view, but it changes something it cannot know from the case data alone. As the human reviewer, I can check internal company context. Here, this Singapore address is actually a corporate VPN exit. So, I added that context into the shared case. Afterwards, I prompt the agent to read the updated state and change its assessment. Singapore is no longer the evidence of compromise. Now, the agent has changed the assessment. Singapore is now no longer the evidence of compromise. Human knowledge changed the reasoning without rewriting the entire case, and we can see every documented step that the agent took. This is essential because it allows the human reviewer to detect suspicious AI behavior, investigate incidents, and identify any mistakes. This allows the AI agent to operate in transparency. Now, the case move into respond to view, and Web MCP changes what the agent can do. Investigation write-up disappears. The agent can read the case and propose a response, but it cannot authorize or execute one. Now, we can see that the agent proposed that we disconnect Don Really and explains its reasons. Simply putting a proof button to authorize the action would not be enough as a browser agent may have browser control skills enabled, which enables them to click on websites normally. We actually separate them into three things: who the user is, whether that user is approving this exact action, and who actually performs it. After the action, the agent reads the change file again. It checks the missing risk instead of assuming the incident is solved, then proposes closure with answer that is still recorded. So, basically, in conclusion, Trust Layer is for teams building agent-ready apps where mistakes can have real consequences. The agent handles investigation while the human adds local knowledge and controls key decisions. And systems only performs approved action where MCP keeps those capabilities limited to what the agent is able to do at each step.

live_observation.first_impression: TraceLayer shows a security incident case, capability boundary, evidence/activity tabs, and a prominent prompt for starting an agent investigation.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked Copy prompt in the Start the investigation with the Agent section.
live_observation.after_state: The button changed to Copied. The case remained available, while the page also offered Sign in with ChatGPT for authenticated interaction.
live_observation.notes: The demo is viewable without login, but the full agent investigation may require ChatGPT sign-in.
